reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Characterised by progressive loss of knowledge of the meaning of words and objects, with fluent but empty speech and prominent anomia
Single-word comprehension is impaired and patients may ask what familiar words mean, yet speech remains fluent and grammatically correct
It is the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia and usually reflects frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology
Surface dyslexia, with difficulty reading irregularly spelled words, is a characteristic feature
Imaging shows asymmetrical, often left-predominant, anterior temporal lobe atrophy, sometimes described as a knife-edge pattern
Right-predominant cases may present with prosopagnosia and behavioural or emotional change rather than language failure
Repetition and speech production are relatively preserved, helping to distinguish it from other aphasia variants
reference.pathophysiology: Semantic dementia is the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia, caused by neurodegeneration focused on the anterior temporal lobes, which serve as a hub for conceptual and semantic knowledge. The commonest underlying pathology is frontotemporal lobar degeneration associated with abnormal TDP-43 protein aggregation. Progressive loss of neurones in the anterior temporal cortex erodes the store of meaning for words, objects and, in right-predominant cases, faces, while the more posterior and perisylvian regions supporting fluent speech output, grammar and repetition remain relatively intact until later. This produces fluent, well-articulated but semantically empty speech with severe naming and comprehension deficits.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex or limbic encephalitis affecting the temporal lobes
Temporal lobe tumour or structural lesion
additionalInvestigations: Speech and language assessment demonstrating impaired single-word comprehension with fluent output
MRI of the brain showing asymmetrical anterior temporal atrophy
FDG-PET to demonstrate anterior temporal hypometabolism
Amyloid PET or cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers to exclude Alzheimer pathology
Neuropsychological testing of semantic knowledge, naming and reading of irregular words
Genetic testing where a family history of frontotemporal dementia is present
redFlags: Subacute onset or systemic features suggesting an inflammatory or infective encephalitis rather than degeneration
Rapid progression inconsistent with the usual course
Prominent behavioural disturbance affecting safety, especially in right-predominant cases
Focal deficits or headache raising concern for a structural lesion
reference.prognosis: Semantic dementia progresses over years, with widening loss of conceptual knowledge and eventual emergence of behavioural change and broader cognitive decline; prognosis reflects the underlying frontotemporal lobar degeneration, and management is supportive with speech and language and behavioural strategies.
pitfalls: Mistaking fluent, empty speech for preserved language and underestimating the comprehension deficit
Attributing the picture to Alzheimer disease rather than recognising the anterior temporal atrophy pattern
Overlooking a treatable temporal-lobe encephalitis in atypical or subacute presentations
Failing to recognise right-predominant cases presenting with prosopagnosia and behavioural change
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Provide speech and language therapy focused on communication strategies and personalised word and picture aids to compensate for semantic loss, as no disease-modifying therapy exists
Manage emerging behavioural and emotional change with non-pharmacological strategies, reserving judicious SSRIs for distressing symptoms and avoiding antipsychotics where possible
Offer occupational therapy, dietetic input for altered eating behaviour, and structured social care for progressive functional decline
Avoid cholinesterase inhibitors, which are ineffective, and distinguish the disorder from Alzheimer pathology to prevent inappropriate treatment
Monitor for dysphagia, safety risks, and carer strain, with proactive advance care planning as conceptual knowledge widens
Refer for genetic counselling and testing where there is a family history of frontotemporal dementia
Coordinate multidisciplinary and specialist cognitive-neurology follow-up to guide supportive care as the disease progresses
